newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Ruling parties claim big win in Yugoslav polls.
newsitem.headline: Ruling parties claim big win in Yugoslav polls.

text.p: The ruling coalition in rump Yugoslavia on Tuesday claimed a "resounding victory" in federal elections and said it had won almost two-thirds of parliamentary seats.

The federal election commmission said by late Monday evening the coalition had secured 50 seats in Sunday's poll, the opposition Zajedno (Together) alliance 21 and the ultra-nationalist Serbian Radical Party 13
No new official figures were available by Tuesday afternoon, but a coalition spokesman, Ivica Dacic, told a news conference that, with 80 percent of the vote counted, they had won at least 64 seats.
"The general tendency is that our lists are winning twice as many votes as all the others combined.

"(The coalition) has won a resounding victory. Together with the DPS (Democratic Party of Socialists) of Montenegro, it will guarantee another four years of development in peace and a stable functioning of the federal parliament's Chamber of Citizens," Dacic said.

However, preliminary projections indicated the goverment could fall six or seven seats short of a two-thirds majority of 93 seats in the 138-seat Chamber of Citizens, which they need to be able to amend the constitution.
Voters across Yugoslavia, which comprises Serbia and Montenegro, went to the polls to choose a new federal parliament, a republican assembly for Montenegro and local councils across the federation.

A tough campaign fought by the leftist coalition, comprising Serbian president Slobodan Milosevic's Socialist Party (SPS), the Yugoslav United Left (JUL) led by his powerful wife Mirjana, and New Democracy, had paid off handsomely, diplomats said.
Although the opposition Zajedno coalition fared worse than expected, it claimed a small victory in blocking the two-thirds majority.

"After the disgraceful (state) media blockade, the removal of opponents of the regime from voters' registers and the ejection of our representatives (from polling booths), the result we achieved in these elections is a miracle," Zajedno spokesman Ivan Kovacevic told a news conference.

Opposition officials blamed their poor performance on the tightly-controlled state-run media, a boycott by ethnic Albanians which gave the governing coalition 15 seats on a platter, a lack of interest in the West and voter apathy.

Diplomats said there was still a chance that the government could win the support of the Radicals to amend the constitution to invest the largely ceremonial post of federal president with new executive powers.
Milosevic, who is widely considered the real power-broker in Yugoslavia, is then expected to move into that job from his current post as Serbian President.
